canonical_topic: Location spread trade example: NP-15 vs. MID-C on an early snowmelt view
definition: A worked example of a March location spread between California (NP-15) and the Pacific Northwest (MID-C) built on a forecast of an earlier-than-normal Cascade snowmelt.
core_idea: A trader who believes government meteorologists' early-thaw forecast is correct, and that the market hasn't priced it in, goes long NP-15 and short MID-C futures to bet that California prices will be relatively higher than Pacific Northwest prices for March.
key_points: Normally, Pacific Northwest power prices hit their seasonal low in April when Cascade snowmelt forces hydro dams to run at full capacity around the clock to avoid flooding, regardless of demand — this generation cannot be curtailed.
The trader's thesis: forecast warm Pacific water temperatures will bring an early thaw, pulling this low-price, must-run hydro period earlier than the market expects.
Trade structure: buy NP-15 peak power futures (long California) and sell MID-C peak power futures (short Pacific Northwest) for the March contract.

A key risk the author flags: natural gas is the marginal fuel in California, so if gas prices fall, California power prices fall too, working against the long NP-15 leg independent of the snowmelt thesis.

The author also questions the spread structure itself: an early warm front and cheap Columbia River hydro power is more likely to push California prices down than up, suggesting an outright short MID-C position might carry less risk than the spread.
Because there is no transmission link being used, the position must be closed by an offsetting futures trade before expiration — it cannot be settled by physically delivering power.
relationships: Depends on marginal-fuel price transmission (gas -> California power)
trading_implications: Profit or loss is realized only if futures prices move in the expected direction by the time the position is liquidated, and liquidation must occur before contract expiration.
A directional (outright) trade can sometimes be a lower-risk expression of a market view than a spread, if the two legs' expected price responses to the same event are not actually offsetting.
caveats: Choosing a spread trade isn't automatically lower risk than an outright position — if the underlying event is expected to move both legs in the same direction, the spread structure itself may be the wrong trade design.
